analysis.one_liner: Lets employers pay any worker who receives tips the lower "tipped" minimum wage, averaging over periods the employer picks.
analysis.headline: The House committee cleared the bill 19-15 and brought it to the floor under a rule barring amendments, but after a near party-line 209-215 vote on January 13, 2026, the final vote was postponed and the bill has not passed.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, an employer can pay a tipped worker less than the $7.25 minimum wage — as little as $2.13 an hour in cash — as long as tips bring the worker up to at least the minimum wage, and only workers whose jobs customarily involve tips qualify. This bill strikes the occupation requirement, so any worker who receives tips counts as "tipped," and it lets the employer choose the measuring period (a day, a pay period, up to 28 days) for making sure tips plus wages add up to minimum wage. The practical effect is that restaurant and hospitality employers can pay the subminimum cash wage to more workers, including kitchen and support staff who get pooled tips, and can average out slow stretches over longer periods.
analysis.who_benefits: Restaurant and hospitality employers, who would be able to pay the lower tip-credit cash wage to a much wider group of workers — regardless of what those workers actually do — and to count tips against the minimum wage over an employer-chosen period rather than ensuring the floor in each pay stretch. Employer groups that have long sought broader use of the tip credit are the clear beneficiaries.

how_it_helps.text: The bill redefines "tipped employee" without regard to the worker's duties, so any worker who receives tips and cash wages that together reach the minimum wage over a work period counts as tipped and can be paid the lower tip-credit cash wage under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

The measuring period — a day, a week, every 2 weeks, every 28 days, or any pay period — is determined by the employer, so tips only have to bring a worker up to the minimum wage on average across a period the employer picks, not period by period.

analysis.who_pays: Tipped and tip-pooling workers. Workers whose jobs are not primarily tipped — such as kitchen staff, bussers, or support staff who receive pooled tips — could have their guaranteed cash wage cut to the subminimum tip-credit rate, and any worker could fall below the minimum wage for days or weeks at a time as long as tips average out over the employer's chosen period. Tips from customers would effectively substitute for wages the employer would otherwise owe.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the requirement that a worker's job customarily involve tips, so employees who do mostly non-tipped work can be paid the reduced tip-credit cash wage as long as pooled tips average out over the period.

Because the employer chooses the measuring period, a worker could earn below the federal minimum wage for stretches of days or weeks and have no claim to back pay as long as the whole period averages out at or above the minimum wage.

Supporters argue the change matches how restaurants actually run tip pools and reduces disputes over which duties count as tipped work; the cost is that the wage floor currently guaranteed to tipped workers becomes an average, not a guarantee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow almost entirely to employers in the form of lower wage obligations, while the risk — a thinner wage floor, shifted onto customers' tips — falls on the roughly millions of workers covered by the tip credit. Despite the name "Tipped Employee Protection Act," the bill's operative provisions expand employer use of the tip credit rather than adding protections for employees. The averaging provision is the most consequential change: it converts a per-period minimum-wage guarantee into an employer-set average.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared committee 19-15, was reported to the House, and was debated under a rule allowing no amendments, but after a close 209-215 vote on a Democratic motion to recommit the House postponed final action and the bill sits without a final passage vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Womack introduced the bill on March 24, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, where it sat for about eight months.

On November 20, 2025, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported as amended by a 19-15 vote; it was formally reported on December 30, 2025, with House Report 119-420, and placed on the Union Calendar.
The Rules Committee reported H. Res. 988, providing that H.R. 2312 be considered under a closed rule — one hour of debate and no amendments from the floor other than one motion to recommit.

On January 13, 2026, the House debated the bill; Rep. Budzinski moved to recommit it to committee, and the motion failed 209-215, with all 209 voting Democrats in favor and all 215 voting Republicans opposed.
After the vote, the Chair announced that further proceedings on the bill were postponed, and no final passage vote has been held; the Congress is still in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No final outcome yet. So far, restaurant and hospitality employers are closer to a law that would let them pay the subminimum cash wage to more workers, while tipped workers are still covered by the current rules — including the guarantee that tips bring them up to the minimum wage — because the bill has not passed.

for.name: 6 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Baumgartner, Sessions, Westerman, Grothman, Letlow, Messmer).

for.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill and ordered it reported as amended, 19-15, on November 20, 2025.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported H. Res. 988 giving the bill a closed rule — one hour of debate, no floor amendments.

for.name: Restaurant and hospitality employers
for.role: Beneficiaries of an expanded tip credit
for.what_they_did: Restaurant industry groups have long pressed Congress to broaden use of the tip credit, including applying it to back-of-house workers; the bill's changes track those requests.

against.name: 209 of 217 House Democrats
against.role: House Democrats voting on the motion to recommit
against.what_they_did: Voted unanimously (209-0 among voting Democrats) for Rep. Budzinski's motion to recommit the bill to committee, which would have allowed further changes; the motion failed 209-215.

against.name: Rep. Nikki Budzinski
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to the Committee on Education and Workforce during floor debate on January 13, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: On the motion to recommit, every voting Democrat (209) voted yes and every voting Republican (215) voted no — a perfect party split.

industries.note: The bill lets restaurants pay the subminimum tip-credit cash wage to any worker who receives tips, including back-of-house staff doing mostly non-tipped work, and to count tips against the minimum wage over an employer-chosen period. The saving comes out of workers' guaranteed cash wages, with customers' tips filling the gap.
Hospitality employers with tip pools could classify more of their workforce as "tipped" under the new duty-blind definition and average tips against the minimum wage over periods the employer sets.

analysis.trajectory: The bill was pulled from a final vote after the motion to recommit showed only a 6-vote margin, which suggests the majority lacks comfortable passage votes with absences. If leaders can line up the votes, a final House vote under the closed rule is the next step; even if it passes, it would then need Senate action, where wage bills of this kind typically stall without a floor vote.
